tier_reason: The README Performance Analysis table (Native 7.0 ns / 32.7 ms, SSE2 6.0 ns / 27.2 ms, SSE2 + fast-math 6.0 ns / 26.8 ms, x87 8.0 ns / 34.8 ms) comes from the public harness test/benchmark.cpp (native baseline in test/benchmark_native_expressions.h, -O3 -DNDEBUG per CMakeLists.txt), but it names neither the compiler (the CI matrix runs both GCC and Clang on ubuntu-latest) nor the runner's CPU model, so it is first-party with partial methodology. The table was added in commit cb358747 (2026-01-11) and is unchanged since, so it predates the 2026-06-10 report of the B1 SSE2 libm-call miscompilation that was later fixed, which also caps it at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table on GitHub Actions CI (Ubuntu runner, 44,229 expressions): average evaluation 6.0 ns for the SSE2 backend versus 7.0 ns for natively compiled code; total evaluation 27.2 ms versus 32.7 ms (1.20x, derived from page data); SSE2 plus fast-math 6.0 ns and 26.8 ms (1.22x, derived from page data); x87 backend 8.0 ns and 34.8 ms, slower than native (0.94x, derived from page data); average compile time 174 us per expression for SSE2 and 135 us for x87. README: the SSE2 backend 'performs on par with or faster than native compiler-generated code'.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from a GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner with no CPU model; the CI matrix builds the benchmark with both GCC and Clang (-O3 -DNDEBUG) and the README does not say which produced the table. The table was written in commit cb358747 (2026-01-11, 'Add SSE2 scalar backend') and has not been re-measured since; the repository's own analysis/improvement_report.md (2026-06-10, a 35-agent analysis run) later found master bugs including B1, a miscompilation in emit_sse2_libm_binary_call where a binary libm call at virtual-stack depth 3 received (arg2, arg2) (logb(a, b + logb(2,x)) returned 2.321928 instead of 2.807355), B2 (the documented '>' operator threw at parse time), B3 (one leaked executable page per constant fold) and B4 (SSE4.1 roundsd emitted with no CPUID gate, so it crashes on pre-SSE4.1 CPUs); current mexce.h has the corrected B1 register move but still no CPUID check for roundsd. The averages are whole nanoseconds (6 versus 7 ns is a one-count difference), so the total-eval ratio of 1.20x is the more precise figure. Fairness: the native baseline is one static function per expression called through a function-pointer table and built with -O3 but no -march, -msse4.1 or -fno-math-errno flag, so the compiler cannot emit roundsd for floor/ceil/round/trunc while mexce does; part of the win may come from that ISA difference. The run_benchmarks target uses 100 iterations per expression with a median of 7 round-robin rounds. There is no comparison with other expression evaluators or JITs (exprtk, muparser, tinyexpr, asmjit-based evaluators), so the claim is parity with native code, not a win over a competitor. analysis/asmd_optimizer_benchmark_summary.csv (an earlier stage) lists avg_runtime_ns 11 to 12 against compiler_runtime_ns 10 to 11, i.e. slower than native then. analysis/performance_acceptance.md (GCC 13.3.0, Clang 18.1.3, MSVC 19.44) reports evaluate medians of 6.5 to 7.6 ns but compares only mexce commits against each other, not against native code. 6 stars, single author.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly and the harness is real (JIT code called through a function pointer, results checked against a SymPy reference, no no-op timing), so confirm at C. Shortcomings to record: compiler and CPU unstated; table measured on January 2026 code that predates the B1 SSE2 libm-call miscompilation fix; native baseline built without -msse4.1 while mexce emits roundsd with no CPUID gate; parity-level gain (1.20x on totals, x87 slower than native); no comparison with other expression JITs.

tier_reason: The README compares libdivide against hardware division with sample output from the public benchmark program (test/benchmark.cpp and test/benchmark.h), but the sample names no CPU, compiler or integer width, so it is first-party with partial methodology. The author's 2021 blog post 'Benchmarking division and libdivide on Apple M1 and Intel AVX512' (blocked here, snippet only) names an Intel Xeon 8275CL at 3.0 GHz; if that post also states compiler and flags it could support A on a later paper-access retier.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'a speedup of up to 10x for 64-bit integer division and a speedup of up to 5x for 32-bit integer division', more with SSE2/AVX2/AVX512/NEON/SVE vectors. README sample output (integer type, CPU and compiler not stated; the benchmark's default type is u64): for divisor 1 (algo 0, no magic number) hardware divide 9.684 ns versus libdivide scalar 0.792 ns (12.2x, derived from page data) and vector 0.426 ns (22.7x, derived from page data); powers of two 2 and 4 (also algo 0) give 11.5 to 11.6x scalar and 21.3x vector (derived from page data); for divisors 3, 5 and 6 (algo 1, multiply-by-magic-number path) libdivide scalar 1.349 to 1.355 ns versus 9.074 to 9.078 ns (6.7x, derived from page data), vector 1.334 ns (6.8x, derived from page data) and branchfree 1.609 ns (5.6x, derived from page data). Author's 2021 blog (snippet only): Intel Xeon 8275CL, divisor 7, u64 hardware 6.998 ns versus libdivide scalar 0.891 ns (7.9x, derived) and AVX512 0.492 ns; u32 hardware 2.298 ns versus scalar 0.872 ns (2.6x, derived).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build by default (CMake's -O3 -DNDEBUG on GCC/Clang) with -march=native when supported, -fno-lax-vector-conversions, and compiler auto-vectorization disabled for the benchmark target (-fno-tree-vectorize on GCC, -fno-vectorize on Clang, chosen by the C compiler's ID); compiler not stated for the README sample.
corrections.workload: Sum of quotients of an array of random numerators divided by one runtime divisor (benchmark default type u64; u16/s16/u32/s32/s64 selectable), timed for hardware division and for libdivide scalar, branchfree, vector and vector-branchfree dividers plus divider generation; minimum of 30 runs per divisor, with every libdivide result checked against the hardware quotient sum.
corrections.caveats: First-party claim. The benchmark program is public, but the README's sample output names no CPU, compiler or integer width, so it is tier C. The largest ratios in the sample (12.2x scalar, 22.7x vector) are for divisor 1 and powers of two, where libdivide reduces to a shift; ordinary divisors on the multiply path give about 6.7x scalar in the same sample, and the README sample omits algo 2 divisors (those needing the add step, such as 7), which the author's 2021 blog (snippet only, Xeon 8275CL) measured at 7.9x for u64 and 2.6x for u32. Generating a divider costs 29 ns for multiply-path divisors in the sample, about three hardware divides, so the divisor must be reused. The README's 90-cycle 64-bit divide latency describes older x86 parts; recent Intel and AMD cores and Apple M1 have much faster dividers (the author's own M1 benchmark post and a 2021 D-forum thread, snippet only, discuss this), so the 10x figure is likely smaller on current hardware (not measured here). The baseline is the compiler-emitted hardware divide for the built-in '/' operator with a runtime divisor, not a C++ library facility. An independent user report on an AMD Zen+ CPU (D forum, snippet only, unverified) gave u32 1.156 ns hardware versus 0.399 ns libdivide.

notes: Numbers are on the README and the harness is sound (checked results, minimum of 30 runs, scalar auto-vectorization disabled), so confirm at C; I corrected claimed_speedup because the 12.2x and 22.7x headline figures come from divisor 1 (and the 'generic algorithm' label was wrong: algo 1 is the multiply-by-magic path). Shortcomings to record: README sample has no CPU, compiler or integer type; headline ratios from trivial divisors; divider generation cost about three divides; the 90-cycle premise is dated on current CPUs. libdivide.com, ridiculousfish.com, forum.dlang.org and lists.puremagic.com were EGRESS_BLOCKED; blog figures are from search snippets only.
